extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, mathematics, physics, and educated readers interested in foundations of space and perception
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing conceptual constructs (space, continuity, sameness, points, lines) by distinguishing perceptual vs conceptual status and judging concepts by their empirical applicability and utility for description, classification, and prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish groups of sense-impressions from their order (objects vs space)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The reader must distinguish carefully between the groups of sense-impressions themselves and the order in which we perceive them to coexist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'objects' as groups of sense-impressions and 'space' as the order/mode in which those groups are perceived. Avoid attributing independent ontological existence to space in the same way as to objects (do not treat space as a 'thing' containing objects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Space is a mode of perception, not an independent thing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Space is an order or mode of perceiving objects, but it has no existence if objects are withdrawn..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret space as conditioned by the perceptive faculty (a mode of presentation). Explanations that treat empty space as an objective immensity are misleading; consider instead perceptual origin and intersubjective similarity as arising from common perceptive faculties or social/biological coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate conceptions by their service in description, classification, and prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: "What we must ask is: How far are these conceptions of service in enabling us to briefly describe and classify our perceptions; how far do they aid us in mentally storing up past experience as a guide for future action?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge scientific concepts (points, lines, atoms, etc.) primarily by their utility: parsimony (brief description), breadth (range of phenomena described), accuracy in classification, and effectiveness in predicting or guiding action, even when they are not perceptual entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate perception from conception; require empirical appeal for perceptual reality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Because we conceive a thing, we must not argue that it is either possible or probable as a perception... The appeal to experience can alone determine whether a conception is possible as a perception."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that conceivability implies perceptual possibility. Use empirical observation and experiment to test whether conceptual constructs correspond to possible perceptions; retain purely conceptual entities as provisional tools until experience warrants treating them as perceptual realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical ideas involve absolute sameness and continuity (ideal limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The geometrical ideas of line and plane involve absolute sameness in all their elements and absolute continuity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that geometric entities (straight line, plane) are idealized limits that presuppose absolute sameness/continuity; assess their applicability by checking whether real perceptions approximate these ideals and whether using them improves description/prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a geometrical framework by descriptive breadth and parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: "From these types we select that one which will enable us to describe the widest range of phenomena in the briefest possible formula, or which will enable us with the greatest accuracy to classify the differences between groups of sense-impressions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing axioms or a geometrical model, prefer the system that balances simplicity (brief formulae) with the greatest range and accuracy in describing/classifying perceptual phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that the mind can conceive beyond perceptual limits; judge such conceptions by empirical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: "The mind is not limited to perceptual association... The scientific value of such conceptions... must in every case be judged by the extent to which they enable us to classify, describe, and predict phenomena."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow conceptual extrapolations (e.g., points, infinitesimals, infinite number) as mental tools, but maintain that their scientific legitimacy rests on their usefulness in organizing experience and producing successful predictions, not on conceivability alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate perceptual divisibility with conceptual infinite divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "The space of our perceptions... is not 'infinitely divisible.' The limit to its divisibility is the limit to our power of perceiving things apart."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the finite divisibility observable in perception (limited by sensory resolution and instruments) from the mathematical notion of infinite divisibility; avoid importing conceptual infinitesimals into claims about perceptual reality without empirical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'sameness' as a practical/conceptual ideal, not an empirical absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: "So far as our perceptual experience goes, probably no two groups of sense-impressions are exactly the same... Yet, as a conception, the sameness of two groups of sense-impressions is a very valid idea, and the basis of much of our scientific classification."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sameness as a useful ideal for classification and practical identification while acknowledging that exact identity rarely (if ever) occurs in perception; scale your criterion of sameness to the level of examination required for the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let empirical science (e.g., physics/chemistry) correct intuitive notions of continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The physicist and the chemist bring many arguments to show us that the finite process of division which suggests continuity would, if carried to an infinite limit, show bodies to be discontinuous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to revise intuitive or naive concepts (e.g., continuity of matter) in light of experimental evidence and theoretical developments; use instruments (microscope, spectroscope, etc.) and scientific argument to test conceptual extrapolations.
